content: Rifaximin is an antibiotic used to treat diarrhea caused by Escherichia coli (commonly referred to as traveler's diarrhea). However, it is not effective in cases of diarrhea accompanied by fever, bloody stools (hematochezia), or diarrhea caused by pathogens other than E. coli. It is also ineffective against traveler's diarrhea caused by Campylobacter jejuni or diarrhea associated with Clostridium difficile. Its efficacy in treating traveler's diarrhea caused by Shigella or Salmonella species has not been established. If symptoms worsen or persist beyond 24 to 48 hours, the medication should be discontinued. There is a potential risk of pseudomembranous colitis, a severe intestinal condition, which may occur during or even weeks to months after treatment. Rifaximin is classified as pregnancy category C, meaning it should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, as there is insufficient evidence regarding its safety. It is unknown whether the drug passes into breast milk, so it should not be used while nursing unless advised otherwise by a healthcare provider. The medication is primarily excreted in the feces (over 90%) and has a half-life of 2 to 5 hours. It can be taken with or without food. Peak plasma levels are typically reached within one hour of administration. Rifaximin induces the enzyme CYP3A4 in liver cells in vitro. When using rifaximin, it is important to follow the prescribed dosage and complete the full course of treatment, even if symptoms improve after a few days. For traveler's diarrhea, if symptoms persist beyond 1 to 2 days, or if bloody diarrhea or fever occurs, consult a doctor immediately. Common side effects are generally mild, but rare severe reactions, such as an allergic response or C. difficile-associated diarrhea, may occur. If severe symptoms like fainting or difficulty breathing arise, seek emergency medical attention. Before starting rifaximin, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, other rifamycin antibiotics (e.g., rifampin, rifabutin), or any inactive ingredients in the product. Additionally, rifaximin may reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Store the medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication as instructed by your pharmacist. Do not flush it down the toilet or pour it into a drain unless directed to do so. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about rifaximin. Always consult your healthcare provider for personalized advice and complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
